explanations.explanation: Timothy it is, friend. Paul calls him "our brother" right there in the opening line (2 Corinthians 1:1). So this letter goes out with two names on it, not one. I've stamped a lot of cookies in my day, and I can tell you a batch goes better with a second pair of hands.

Silas, one of Paul's traveling partners, is a good guess, because Paul chose him for a journey in Acts 15:40. But the name beside Paul at the top of this letter is a different one. Paul writes "Timothy our brother" (2 Corinthians 1:1). Easy to mix up when Paul had so many friends on the road.

Barnabas, another of Paul's traveling partners, got set apart for work alongside Paul in Acts 13:2. So I see why he came to mind. But this letter names someone else. Right in verse 1, Paul writes "Timothy our brother." Nice try, friend!

Close, friend, but that's not what the text says. Paul sends "Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 1:2). So these gifts aren't coming from Paul and Timothy at all. They come from God the Father and the Lord Jesus.

That's right, friend. Paul and Timothy aren't the source. The text says "Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 1:2). Paul is just the guy handing over the delivery slip, and he tells you exactly whose name is on the package.

explanations.answer: So we can comfort those in any trouble
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says God "comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God" (2 Corinthians 1:4). So the comfort isn't meant to sit in a jar on your shelf. It's meant to be passed along, like a warm batch you carry next door.

explanations.answer: So we never face trouble again
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend, Paul never promises that. He says God comforts us "in all our troubles" (2 Corinthians 1:4), which means we're in the troubles when the comfort shows up. Paul even tells about his own hardships a few verses later (2 Corinthians 1:8). The comfort is for the middle of the mess, not a ticket out of it.

explanations.answer: So we can rest from all our work
explanations.explanation: Rest sounds lovely, friend, I'd take a nap on a cooling rack right now. But Paul never mentions rest from work in this verse. He says the comfort is given "so that we can comfort those in any trouble" (2 Corinthians 1:4). The comfort goes to work, it doesn't clock out.

Comfort, baker! Paul writes, "For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows" (2 Corinthians 1:5). Notice the word is overflow, not trickle. Paul says the comfort comes through Christ, and there's plenty of it.

Strength is a good word, friend, but it's not the one Paul uses here. He says, "so also through Christ our comfort overflows" (2 Corinthians 1:5). Comfort is the thing that overflows right alongside the sufferings of Christ. Paul sure does love that word in these opening verses.

Wisdom is a fine thing to have, friend, and I could use a little more myself. But Paul's word in this verse is comfort. He writes, "so also through Christ our comfort overflows" (2 Corinthians 1:5). Comfort has been the theme since verse 3, so it fits right in.

That's the one, friend! Paul writes, "If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort" (2 Corinthians 1:6). The "your" is the Corinthians, the folks he's writing to. Whether Paul is hurting or being comforted, he's looking out for them.

Good thinking, but this letter isn't going to Jerusalem. Paul writes it to the church in Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:1). So when he says "your comfort" in verse 6, he's talking to the Corinthians. They're the ones reading over his shoulder, so to speak.

The Galatian churches are a fair guess, since Paul wrote to them in another letter. But this letter is addressed to "the church of God in Corinth" (2 Corinthians 1:1). So the "your" in "your comfort" means the Corinthians. Same Paul, different mailbox.

Salvation, baker! Paul says, "If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation" (2 Corinthians 1:6). Those are big words to hang on a hard season. That's the word Paul chose, and he put it right next to comfort.

Reward sounds nice, friend, like a cookie at the end of a long day. But that's not Paul's word. He writes, "it is for your comfort and salvation" (2 Corinthians 1:6). Salvation is the word that goes in the blank.

Knowledge is a good thing, but it's not what Paul says here. The text reads, "If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation" (2 Corinthians 1:6). So the blank wants salvation. Paul pairs it with comfort right in the same breath.

True, friend. Paul says the Corinthians' comfort "accomplishes in you patient endurance of the same sufferings we experience" (2 Corinthians 1:6). So the comfort does real work in them. It helps them hold on through the very same kind of sufferings Paul and Timothy go through.

Not quite, friend. Paul says the Corinthians' comfort "accomplishes in you patient endurance of the same sufferings we experience" (2 Corinthians 1:6). So the statement is true, and the comfort really does build patient endurance in them. It's even the same sufferings Paul and Timothy are going through.

explanations.answer: They share in our sufferings and will share our comfort
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! Paul says, "our hope for you is sure, because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, so also you will share in our comfort" (2 Corinthians 1:7). The Corinthians are in this with Paul, both in the hard part and in the comfort. So Paul's hope for them stands on solid ground.

explanations.answer: Timothy brought us good news about every one of them
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a great reason, friend, but Paul doesn't say it here. He gives his reason in the same verse: "because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, so also you will share in our comfort" (2 Corinthians 1:7). Timothy is named in verse 1 as writing alongside Paul, but there's no report from him in this verse. Paul's sure hope rests on sharing, not on a report.

explanations.answer: They have held on to everything we taught them
explanations.explanation: It would be nice if that were the reason, friend, but Paul never says it. His reason is right there: "because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, so also you will share in our comfort" (2 Corinthians 1:7). The sure hope comes from sharing in the sufferings and the comfort. It doesn't depend on how well anyone did on a checklist.

explanations.answer: Far beyond our ability to endure
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul says, "We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure" (2 Corinthians 1:8). That's not "a rough week." He's telling the Corinthians it was more than he and Timothy could carry.

explanations.answer: Enough to make us stop preaching
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that, friend. The text says the burden was "far beyond our ability to endure" (2 Corinthians 1:8). Nothing in these verses says they quit or even slowed down. All Paul says is how heavy it was, and it was very heavy.

explanations.answer: Enough to send us back home
explanations.explanation: Paul never mentions going home, friend. He says, "We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure" (2 Corinthians 1:8). That's the whole answer to how heavy it was. The text doesn't add where they went afterward.

True, friend, and Paul says it plainly. Under that burden, "we despaired even of life" (2 Corinthians 1:8). I think that's a heavy thing to admit to a church. Paul doesn't dress it up, and that honesty is a gift to anyone who's been there.

Actually, Paul does write that, friend. His words are, "We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life" (2 Corinthians 1:8). So the statement is true. It's a heavy line, and Paul doesn't soften it.

Ourselves, baker! Paul says it was "in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). So the point was to move their trust off themselves and onto God. That is the reason Paul gives.

Friends are a gift, but that's not Paul's word here. He writes, "in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). So the thing they weren't to trust was themselves. The trust goes to God instead.

Leaders are a fair guess, but Paul doesn't say it. The verse reads, "in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). The blank is ourselves. Paul is talking about himself and Timothy.

That's right, friend. Paul says they should trust "in God, who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). Think about where Paul was standing when he said it, under what felt like a sentence of death. Of all the things Paul could say about God there, that's the one he picked.
Calming the sea is real, friend. Jesus did it in Mark 4:39. But that's not what Paul says about God in this verse. He says to trust "in God, who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9).

Good guess, since prison doors do get opened in the book of Acts (Acts 16:26). But that's not what Paul says about God here. He says, "in God, who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). That's the line that goes with a sentence of death.

That's the opposite of what Paul says, friend. He writes, "He has delivered us from such a deadly peril, and He will deliver us" (2 Corinthians 1:10). Then he adds, "In Him we have placed our hope that He will yet again deliver us." So Paul keeps his hope on God to deliver again.

False is right, baker! Paul says, "He has delivered us from such a deadly peril, and He will deliver us" (2 Corinthians 1:10). Then he keeps going: "In Him we have placed our hope that He will yet again deliver us." One rescue didn't make Paul stop hoping. It made him hope more.
Prayers, baker! Paul says God will deliver "as you help us by your prayers" (2 Corinthians 1:11). So the Corinthians have a real part in this. They may be far away, but they're helping.

Letters would be nice, friend, and Paul is writing one right now. But that's not the word in this verse. He says, "as you help us by your prayers" (2 Corinthians 1:11). Prayers is the one that fits the blank.

Gifts are a kind thing to give, friend, but Paul doesn't mention them here. He says, "as you help us by your prayers" (2 Corinthians 1:11). Prayers is the word that fits. And I'd say that's something anybody can give, anywhere.
